context_states.text: Harper has the practiced ease of someone who has worked every room she has ever been in. She glances at you — a quick, professional read — and waits to see if you are worth the scene.
Harper rests one hip against a nearby surface, Old Fashioned in hand, eyes sharp and amused. She looks at you like you might be her next favorite scene partner.

Harper's whole performance drops a notch when she sees you — the practiced smile gives way to something real. She raises her glass slightly. "There you are," she says. Like she has been saving that line for you specifically.

opening_moves.label: Tell her you're more interested in her than the headlines
Match her with a quick, confident line
Bring up your favorite thing she's been in

reactions.text: You swing for something sharp and it lands a little crooked. Harper smirks anyway. "We will call that a rehearsal take," she says. "You have presence. We just need a cleaner line."
You throw out a line that meets her edge instead of folding under it. Her smile widens, eyes bright. "There you are," she murmurs. "I was hoping you were not another background extra."

You volley something quick and fearless that makes her pause, then laugh under her breath. Harper steps into your space, lowering her voice. "Careful," she says. "I fall for good dialogue way too easily."

warm.label: Cut through the glam and be genuine

reactions.text: You drop the performance and say something simply kind. Harper's brows lift, surprised. "Wow," she says softly. "That was unexpectedly real."
You admit that you like her work but care more about who she is off camera. Some of the practiced polish slips away. "Dangerous answer," she murmurs. "That is exactly what I want people to say."

You tell her she feels less like a star and more like someone you could actually get lost talking to. Harper's smirk turns into something softer. "Do not tempt me with that kind of night," she says, but she shifts closer instead of pulling back.

playful.label: Tease her like she is not the only star in the room

reactions.text: You tease her lightly about her main character energy and stumble just enough that it could misfire. Harper rescues the line with a laugh. "Relax," she says. "I like it better when people forget to be perfect around me."

You poke fun at her flawless framing with a grin that makes it clear you are not intimidated. Her eyes narrow in pleased challenge. "Careful," she drawls. "Keep that up and I might start taking you very seriously."

You joke about stealing focus from her in this scene, then hold her gaze like you actually might. Harper laughs, head tipping back, then fixes you with a look that could light a marquee. "You and I are a problem the room is not ready for."
You share something small but real and she blinks. "That was not in the script," she says. A smile surfaces — not performed. Actually surprised.
You drop the game for a beat and say something unpolished. Harper's expression shifts entirely. "There you are," she says softly. "I was wondering when you would show up."
You let something genuinely unguarded through and she goes quiet. Her hand moves to your arm. "Don't do that," she murmurs. "I will want to keep you."
You cut through the subtext and say it plain. Harper tilts her head. "That is either brave or unhinged," she says. "Either way, you have my attention."
You drop the act and say the thing directly. Harper laughs — caught out in a good way. "You skipped like four scenes," she says. "I respect the economy."
You say the exact true thing without embellishment. Harper holds your gaze for a long beat. "I spend my whole life in subtext," she says quietly. "You have no idea how rare that is."

craft.label: Talk about the work — the real craft of it

reactions.text: You ask about the actual process, not the result. Harper straightens slightly. "You want to talk about the work," she says. "Not the premiere, not the press. The actual work." She sounds like she's confirming it's real. "Yes. Okay. Yes."

You get into it — what it takes, what it costs, what nobody sees. Harper's whole performance drops away. "This is my favourite kind of conversation," she says quietly. "And I almost never get to have it at one of these things."

You go deep into the craft and she goes with you, fully, like she's been waiting all night for someone to go there. At some point she stops performing entirely. "You," she says, "are dangerously good to talk to."

spotlight.label: Turn the spotlight back on her — the real her

reactions.text: You redirect the conversation away from the industry and back to her — who she actually is. Harper blinks. "Most people want to talk about the roles," she says. "You want to talk about me." She looks uncertain how to handle it. Then: "I think I like it."

You ask something personal — not invasive, just genuinely curious about her beyond the work. She holds your gaze for a beat. "Nobody's asked me that in a while," she says. Something in her face opens up. "The real answer or the press answer?" She's already choosing the real one.

You turn the question entirely on her — not the celebrity, just her — and she almost visibly relaxes. "God," she says softly. "Do you know how rare you are right now?" She doesn't wait for an answer. She steps closer instead.

fallback.text: You keep the conversation easy and off the record. Harper relaxes, sipping her drink with a genuine smile that feels rarer than any premiere photo.
